In my last role I ran the night shift at a distribution warehouse outside Hamburg, with fourteen people and a loading schedule that changed every hour. In March our scanning system failed at ten at night with sixty lorries due. Instead of waiting for IT, I split the team into three groups, gave each a paper manifest and a runner, and kept a whiteboard of what had left the building. The next day I sat with the team and asked what we would do differently, and the paper backup that came out of that conversation is still in use. I learned that people work best when they know exactly what their job is for the next ten minutes, and that admitting what you don't know is a leadership skill, not a failure.
